item.title: HiRO-ACEv2 Enables Low‑Cost Global 3 km Climate Simulations with Improved Extreme‑Event Modeling
item.description:
HiRO-ACEv2 Enables Low‑Cost Global 3 km Climate Simulations with Improved Extreme‑Event Modeling

🔍 Overview

We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to the High Resolution Output AI Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. The update focuses on accurately reproducing extreme rain, wind, and pressure events while delivering global 3 km climate data at a fraction of the cost of traditional high‑resolution models.

🧩 How it works

  • HiRO‑ACE (2026) – Consists of two components:
    • ACE – An AI model that runs at a coarse 100 km resolution.
    • HiRO – A downscaling model that sharpens ACE’s output to 3 km detail.
  • HiRO‑ACEv2 – Replaces the original downscaler with HiROv2, which:
    • Predicts several high‑resolution fields simultaneously (rainfall, wind, pressure, etc.) instead of only rainfall.
    • Shows improved skill in predicting the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values.
    • Matches target high‑resolution statistics to within 3 % even for events that occur only once in a million data points.
  • The system is trained on coarsened data from the X‑SHiELD global atmospheric model and inherits its ability to simulate storms and other small‑scale weather.

⚙️ Key details

  • Extreme‑event performance:
    • Accurately estimates total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms never seen during training.
    • Generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands (winds and pressure around the eye are somewhat more lopsided than X‑SHiELD).
    • Realistically produces strong downslope winds on mountain slopes.
  • Cost and speed:
    • Generates global 3 km data at about 1/300th the cost of X‑SHiELD (≈ 300 times cheaper).
    • For a single region, savings can exceed 100 times, depending on area size.
    • A streamlined HiROv2 version under development could be more than ten times faster.
  • Long‑term simulations:
    • A full year of global 3 km data was produced by combining HiROv2 with the updated ACE.
    • Over a 10‑year run, hurricane energy and the distributions of rain, wind, and pressure closely match X‑SHiELD.
    • Average climate patterns and overall statistics remain well aligned with X‑SHiELD.
  • Training updates:
    • Both ACE and HiROv2 were retrained; the new training regime improves reproduction of the most intense events.
    • Current version works only with the ACE tuned to match X‑SHiELD and cannot yet generate high‑resolution data for other climate states.

🚀 Availability

  • The models are downloadable, and tutorial notebooks are provided to guide users through running them.
  • A web demo showcases pre‑generated precipitation, wind, and sea‑level pressure from HiROv1, HiROv2, and X‑SHiELD side‑by‑side, allowing users to zoom in on regions of interest.

💡 Why it matters

HiRO‑ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible, inexpensive way to create many versions of high‑resolution climate fields—including extreme events—over multi‑year periods. The dramatic cost reduction and the ability to simulate rare, intense weather phenomena open new possibilities for climate research, impact assessments, and risk modeling.

#AIClimate #HighResolution #ExtremeEvents #ClimateModeling

Source: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost

item.title: Microsoft releases open-source tool to boost two-to-six-week weather forecasts
item.description:
Microsoft releases open-source tool to boost two-to-six-week weather forecasts

Microsoft Research has unveiled a new machine‑learning tool that corrects systematic bias in existing weather models, extending reliable forecasts out to two‑to‑six weeks.

🔍 Overview

  • Old‑school physics‑based forecasting and current AI models lose reliability beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft says it has solved with machine learning.
  • The tool, called Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC), is now open‑source software and its findings were published today in Nature.
  • Microsoft joins Google, Nvidia and other firms developing AI tools for weather forecasting.

🧩 How it works

  • PBC uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections, rather than building a new standalone weather model.
  • It can run on standard CPUs, avoiding the supercomputer or GPU clusters required by traditional physics‑based or generative‑AI forecasts.
  • Example bias: climate‑change‑induced warming can cause a model that relies on historic records to predict temperatures that are too cold.

📊 Performance

  • Improves the accuracy of the European Centre for Medium‑Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) physics‑based model for 98 % of precipitation targets and 92 % of temperature targets.
  • Doubles the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis.
Model corrected by PBC Reported improvement
ECMWF physics‑based model (precipitation) 98 % of targets more accurate
ECMWF physics‑based model (temperature) 92 % of targets more accurate
ECMWF AI forecasting system Accuracy doubled

🌍 Accessibility & Impact

  • Designed as a lightweight, easy‑to‑train approach that resource‑strained weather agencies can adopt.
  • Runs on CPUs, lowering compute and infrastructure barriers that often exclude agencies in economically developing countries.
  • Aims to give farmers, emergency responders and other stakeholders more certain forecasts for planning.
  • Genevieve Flaspohler notes the method lets scientists without huge pools of resources configure models for specific localities.
  • Flaspohler’s nonprofit Rhiza Research is testing PBC with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority, funded by the Gates Foundation, ahead of an expected extreme rainy season during a record‑breaking El Niño.

🚀 Availability

  • The software is released as open‑source, allowing the broader community to adopt the bias‑correction technique.
  • The research team includes scientists from Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF and other institutions.
  • ECMWF previously recognized the work by awarding it in its AI Weather Quest competition.
  • Matthew Chantry of ECMWF called the paper “a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” while noting the challenge of turning ideas into operational processes.

#WeatherForecasting #MachineLearning #OpenSource #ClimateAI

Source: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
